overview: A table in Unity Catalog is a leaf-level securable in the catalog.schema.table namespace that holds structured data, almost always in the Delta Lake format.

Unity Catalog distinguishes managed tables, whose lifecycle and storage Databricks fully controls, from external tables, which point at data in a location Unity Catalog governs but does not own end-to-end.
Tables are governed with GRANT/REVOKE, carry properties and ownership, and behave differently on DROP depending on whether they are managed or external.
learningObjectives: Distinguish managed from external tables in Unity Catalog and understand the storage and ownership model behind each.
Learn the main table types: managed Delta, external, views, and streaming tables, and when to use each.
Understand how GRANT/REVOKE, table properties, ownership, and DROP behavior work for tables under Unity Catalog governance.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A Unity Catalog table is a securable object at the third level of the namespace (catalog.schema.table) that maps a logical name to a set of data files (typically Delta Lake) plus metadata. A managed table has both its metadata and underlying files governed and lifecycle-controlled by Unity Catalog within a managed location, whereas an external table has Unity-Catalog-governed metadata but its files reside at a user-specified external location whose lifecycle Databricks does not fully own.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: A table is where your rows actually live. With a managed table, Databricks owns the box and the contents — if you throw the box away (DROP), the contents go too. With an external table, Databricks only holds a label pointing to a box you own — throw away the label (DROP) and your box of files stays right where it is.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Legacy Databricks tables in the Hive metastore were workspace-scoped, often external, and governed only by coarse workspace-level access controls. Unity Catalog (GA 2022) re-homed tables into the central account metastore with fine-grained GRANT/REVOKE, standardized on Delta Lake for managed tables, and formalized the managed-vs-external distinction so that storage ownership and DROP semantics became explicit and consistent across all workspaces.

whyItMatters.business: Tables are the assets analysts and applications consume; governing them with fine-grained grants protects sensitive data while data discovery and lineage make trusted tables easy to find and reuse, accelerating analytics.
whyItMatters.engineering: The managed-vs-external choice determines who owns storage layout, optimization, and cleanup. Managed tables let Databricks auto-optimize and safely reclaim files, while external tables integrate with data shared by or with other tools.
whyItMatters.scalability: Delta-backed managed tables support features like automatic file compaction, liquid clustering, and predictive optimization, which keep large tables performant as they grow without manual tuning.
whyItMatters.cost: Managed tables enable automatic cleanup of files after DROP and optimization that reduces small-file overhead, while external tables risk orphaned storage costs if files aren't tracked because Databricks won't delete them on DROP.
whyItMatters.reliability: Centralized ownership, ACID Delta transactions, and consistent DROP semantics prevent the data-loss and orphaned-file surprises common with ad-hoc external tables, and grants ensure only authorized principals read or modify data.

coreComponents.name: Table Metadata (in the metastore)
coreComponents.definition: The logical definition: name, schema/columns, type (managed/external), properties, owner, and pointer to storage.
coreComponents.purpose: To register the table as a governable securable and resolve queries to the right files.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Tracks ownership and grants, table properties, and whether the table is managed or external; lives in the central Unity Catalog metastore.
coreComponents.examples: Owner = data_eng group, type = MANAGED, properties = {delta.enableChangeDataFeed=true}

coreComponents.name: Underlying Data Files (Delta)
coreComponents.definition: The Parquet data files plus the Delta transaction log that physically store the rows.
coreComponents.purpose: To hold the actual data with ACID guarantees, time travel, and schema enforcement.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store rows and the transaction log; for managed tables these sit under the schema/catalog managed location, for external tables at a user-specified external location.

coreComponents.name: Storage Location and Ownership
coreComponents.definition: Where the files live and who controls their lifecycle (Databricks for managed, the user/team for external).
coreComponents.purpose: To define DROP behavior, optimization responsibility, and cleanup ownership.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Managed: Unity Catalog owns layout and deletes files on DROP. External: governed via an external location with permissions, but files persist on DROP.
coreComponents.examples: Managed table cleaned up on DROP; external table's files remain after DROP

internalWorking: On CREATE TABLE without a LOCATION, Unity Catalog creates a managed table and stores its Delta files under the schema's (or catalog's) managed location, recording the table as MANAGED in the metastore.

On CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION '<path>' (or CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE), Unity Catalog creates an external table; the path must fall under a registered external location the principal is authorized to use, and the table is recorded as EXTERNAL.
Every read/write checks the table's ACLs and inherited schema/catalog grants; authorized writes append to the Delta log, providing ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel.

On DROP, a managed table's metadata is removed and its files are scheduled for deletion (subject to retention), whereas an external table only loses its metadata while the files remain at the external location.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Query -> Metastore (resolve catalog.schema.table + check grants) -> Storage (managed location for managed tables, external location for external tables) -> Delta log + Parquet files
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An engineer runs CREATE TABLE sales.gold.orders (...) with no LOCATION, producing a managed Delta table under the schema's managed location.
2. Unity Catalog records it as MANAGED, owned by the data_eng group, and writes the Delta log + Parquet files to the managed path.
3. GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts lets analysts query it (given USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA).
4. A partner dataset already in s3://partner/orders is registered via CREATE TABLE sales.bronze.partner_orders LOCATION 's3://partner/orders' as an external table.
5. DROP TABLE sales.gold.orders deletes both metadata and files; DROP TABLE sales.bronze.partner_orders removes only metadata and leaves the partner files intact.

keyTerminology.meaning: A table whose metadata and underlying files are fully governed and lifecycle-controlled by Unity Catalog within a managed location.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables automatic optimization and safe file cleanup; DROP removes the data files too.

keyTerminology.meaning: A table with Unity-Catalog-governed metadata but files stored at a user-specified external location.
keyTerminology.importance: Used to govern data shared with or owned by other tools; DROP leaves the files in place.

keyTerminology.meaning: A Unity Catalog securable that maps a cloud storage path to a storage credential and controls who can read/write/create there.
keyTerminology.importance: External tables must reside under a registered external location the principal is authorized to use.

importantConcepts.concept: DROP behavior differs by table type
importantConcepts.explanation: Dropping a managed table removes its metadata and deletes its underlying data files (subject to retention/UNDROP windows). Dropping an external table removes only the metadata; the files at the external location are untouched, which prevents accidental data loss but can leave orphaned storage.

Grants on a table can be set directly, but a table also inherits grants from its parent schema and catalog (e.g., GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA). The table owner has full control and can grant/revoke privileges; ownership should sit with a group or service principal, not an individual.

variationsAndTypes: **Managed Delta table:** Default type; files in the managed location, fully governed, eligible for predictive optimization and automatic cleanup.
**External table:** Files at a user-specified external location under a registered external location; DROP leaves files intact.
**View:** A saved query (logical, no stored data) governed as its own securable, used to expose subsets or transformations of tables.
**Streaming table (and materialized view):** Delta/DLT-managed tables that are continuously or incrementally refreshed from a streaming or batch source, used in pipelines.
advantages: **Fine-grained governance:** GRANT/REVOKE at table level (plus schema/catalog inheritance) enforces least privilege.
**ACID + Delta features:** Time travel, schema enforcement, CDF, and optimization come built in for Delta tables.
**Safe lifecycle for managed tables:** Automatic optimization and file cleanup on DROP, with UNDROP for recovery.
**Interoperability via external tables:** Govern data produced or consumed by other engines without copying it.
disadvantages: **External-table cleanup is manual:** DROP leaves files behind, risking orphaned storage costs.
**Managed-table DROP is destructive:** Files are deleted, so accidental drops need UNDROP within the retention window.
**External locations add setup:** External tables require correctly configured external locations and storage credentials.
**Type choice is somewhat sticky:** Converting between managed and external requires deliberate steps, not a simple flag flip.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use managed tables for data Databricks should own end-to-end (most pipeline outputs) to get automatic optimization and safe cleanup. Use external tables when files must be shared with other tools, already exist in a specific location, or must outlive the table definition.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid external tables for routine pipeline outputs where you want automatic optimization and cleanup. Avoid managed tables when the storage must be owned/accessed by external systems or when DROP must not delete the files.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A managed table is like a meal-kit subscription: the company sources, stores, and disposes of everything for you, and cancelling (DROP) ends the deliveries and clears the fridge. An external table is like keeping groceries you bought yourself in your own pantry while the app just tracks them — delete the app entry (DROP) and the groceries stay in your pantry.

commonMisconceptions.myth: DROP TABLE always deletes the data files.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only for managed tables. Dropping an external table removes the metadata but leaves the files at the external location untouched.

commonMisconceptions.myth: All Unity Catalog tables are external because data lives in cloud storage.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Managed tables also live in cloud storage, but in a Unity-Catalog-controlled managed location whose lifecycle Databricks owns; managed is in fact the default and recommended type.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Managed Delta tables benefit from automatic file compaction, liquid clustering, and predictive optimization, keeping large tables performant; partitioning or clustering keys should match common query predicates.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Delta's ACID transactions and schema enforcement prevent partial writes and bad-schema corruption; consistent DROP/UNDROP semantics protect against accidental loss for managed tables.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: The Delta transaction log enables time travel and recovery to prior versions; table metadata in the central metastore survives workspace/cluster failures.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Use system tables and SHOW GRANTS to monitor table access and ownership; track storage growth and small-file counts; monitor for orphaned files left by dropped external tables.
productionConsiderations.security: Apply least privilege with table-level GRANT/REVOKE, prefer group/service-principal ownership, and use row filters and column masks for sensitive columns instead of broad table access.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Managed tables auto-clean files on DROP and optimize layout; external tables require manual cleanup to avoid paying for orphaned storage. OPTIMIZE/VACUUM and predictive optimization control file sprawl.
productionConsiderations.performance: Choose appropriate clustering/partitioning, run OPTIMIZE (or rely on predictive optimization), and set useful table properties (e.g., enabling change data feed only when needed) to balance performance and overhead.

codeExamples.title: Creating managed and external tables
codeExamples.overview: Contrasts a default managed Delta table (no LOCATION) with an external table that points at an existing cloud path under a registered external location.
codeExamples.breakdown: The orders table omits LOCATION, so Unity Catalog makes it MANAGED and writes Delta files under the gold schema's managed location; the TBLPROPERTIES enables Change Data Feed. partner_orders specifies LOCATION, making it EXTERNAL and bound to files under an authorized external location. DESCRIBE EXTENDED reveals the type, location, owner, and properties.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: orders is created as a managed Delta table with CDF enabled; partner_orders is created as an external table referencing the partner path. DESCRIBE EXTENDED shows Type = MANAGED for orders and EXTERNAL for partner_orders.
codeExamples.commonIssues: External CREATE fails if the LOCATION is not under a registered external location the principal can use, or if storage credentials are misconfigured. Managed CREATE fails without CREATE TABLE on the schema.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer managed tables for pipeline outputs to get predictive optimization and automatic cleanup; only enable properties like CDF when a downstream consumer actually needs them.

codeExamples.title: GRANT and REVOKE on tables
codeExamples.overview: Shows table-level access control, including the traversal privileges and how REVOKE removes access.
codeExamples.breakdown: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA let principals traverse to the table. SELECT grants read; SELECT + MODIFY grants read/write. REVOKE removes a previously granted privilege. ALTER TABLE ... OWNER TO assigns ownership to a group, which gains full control. SHOW GRANTS audits effective privileges.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: analysts initially can read orders, then lose read access after the REVOKE; data_eng can read and write and becomes the owner. SHOW GRANTS reflects the final state.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Revoking SELECT on a table does not remove access if the principal still has SELECT inherited from the schema or catalog. Only owners (or those with MANAGE/sufficient privilege) can grant or transfer ownership.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Manage grants at the schema level for broad access and use table-level grants only for exceptions; assign ownership to groups/service principals, never individuals.

codeExamples.title: DROP behavior: managed vs external
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates the key interview point that DROP deletes files for managed tables but not for external tables, and how UNDROP recovers a managed table.
codeExamples.breakdown: Dropping the managed orders table removes its metadata and schedules file deletion; UNDROP restores it within the retention window. Dropping the external partner_orders removes only metadata, so the Delta files persist and the table can be re-created by pointing at the same LOCATION with no data copy.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: After DROP, orders' files are deleted (recoverable via UNDROP for a limited time); partner_orders' files survive and the table is fully restored by re-registering the same external location.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming dropping an external table frees storage (it does not, causing orphaned cost). Assuming a managed DROP is always recoverable after the retention/UNDROP window elapses.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For external tables, explicitly delete files in cloud storage when truly decommissioning. For managed tables, rely on UNDROP for quick recovery but treat DROP in production as destructive.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A data team must serve a curated 'orders' fact table to analysts while also governing a partner-provided dataset that lives in the partner's own bucket, all with least-privilege access and predictable cleanup semantics.
endToEndExample.inputData: Internal order events to be materialized as a managed gold table, and a partner Delta dataset already present at s3://partner-bucket/shared/orders that must be governed but not copied or deleted by Databricks.
endToEndExample.architecture: Unity Catalog catalog sales_catalog with schemas bronze and gold. The internal fact table is a managed Delta table in gold; the partner dataset is an external table in bronze registered against a Unity Catalog external location.
processingSteps: 1. Create the managed gold.orders table (no LOCATION) so Databricks owns storage and optimization.
2. Register the partner dataset as an external table bronze.partner_orders with LOCATION under an authorized external location.
3. Grant USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA broadly, SELECT on gold.orders to analysts, and SELECT+MODIFY to data_eng.
4. Set ownership of both tables to the data_eng group and apply column masks on any sensitive columns.
5. When decommissioning, DROP the managed table (files cleaned automatically, UNDROP available) and DROP the external table (metadata only; partner files preserved).
endToEndExample.output: Analysts query a governed, optimized managed fact table; the partner dataset is queryable and governed without duplicating or risking the partner's files; cleanup is automatic for the managed table and non-destructive for the external one.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Audit access via system.access.audit and SHOW GRANTS; monitor managed-table storage growth and small-file counts; watch for orphaned files if external tables are dropped.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Permission errors are diagnosed by checking USE CATALOG -> USE SCHEMA -> SELECT/MODIFY. External CREATE errors usually mean the LOCATION isn't covered by an authorized external location or the storage credential is wrong.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A governed lakehouse where managed tables give Databricks-owned optimization and safe cleanup, external tables integrate partner data without ownership risk, and table-level grants plus group ownership enforce least privilege — exactly the model interviewers expect you to articulate.

industryUseCases.problem: Curated fact and dimension tables must be performant, optimized, and safely lifecycle-managed for many analysts.
industryUseCases.solution: Store curated outputs as managed Delta tables with predictive optimization, governed by schema- and table-level grants, with masks on PII columns.
industryUseCases.benefits: Automatic optimization and cleanup, fine-grained access, and recoverability via UNDROP if a table is dropped by mistake.

industryUseCases.company: Data sharing with partners and external tools
industryUseCases.problem: Datasets produced by or consumed by external systems must be governed without copying or risking deletion of files.
industryUseCases.solution: Register partner/external data as external tables under controlled external locations, granting read access while ensuring DROP never deletes the partner files.
industryUseCases.benefits: Zero-copy interoperability, governed access, and non-destructive lifecycle that protects externally owned storage.

industryUseCases.problem: Regulated tables require strict least-privilege access, ownership accountability, and full auditability.
industryUseCases.solution: Use managed Delta tables owned by responsible teams, table-level GRANT/REVOKE for least privilege, and audit logs/lineage to prove who accessed what.
industryUseCases.benefits: Demonstrable access control, clear ownership, and ACID guarantees that satisfy auditors.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Managed Delta tables scale via automatic compaction, liquid clustering, and predictive optimization, which handle file sizing without manual OPTIMIZE jobs. Clustering/partition keys should match high-selectivity query predicates to prune data efficiently.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: The Delta transaction log enables time travel and version-level recovery, and centralized metastore metadata survives workspace failures. UNDROP recovers accidentally dropped managed tables within the retention window.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Because table metadata and grants live in the account-level metastore and data sits in durable cloud storage, the same table resolves consistently across all workspaces and regions that share the metastore.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Recreate table definitions from versioned DDL/IaC; managed data is recoverable via time travel and storage durability, while external data persists independently in its own location and is re-registered by pointing at the same path.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Run or enable predictive OPTIMIZE to compact small files, use Z-order/liquid clustering on filter columns, collect statistics, and enable CDF or deletion vectors only when needed to avoid unnecessary overhead.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Managed tables auto-delete files on DROP (no orphaned storage) and auto-optimize layout; external tables require deliberate cleanup of files to avoid paying for orphaned data. Tune VACUUM retention to balance time travel against storage cost.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Enforce least privilege with table-level GRANT/REVOKE plus schema inheritance, use row filters and column masks for sensitive data, prefer group/service-principal ownership, and never grant broad MODIFY where SELECT suffices.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use system.access.audit for access events, system.information_schema for inventory, and DESCRIBE EXTENDED/SHOW GRANTS for per-table checks. Track storage and file counts to spot small-file or orphaned-file problems.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Delta schema enforcement, CHECK constraints, and expectations (in DLT/streaming tables) validate data on write; views and gold tables expose only vetted data to consumers.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Audit logs capture CREATE/DROP/ALTER and GRANT/REVOKE events; alert on drops of production tables, ownership changes, and broad MODIFY grants on sensitive tables.

recommendedPractices: **Default to managed tables:** Use managed Delta tables for pipeline outputs to get automatic optimization and safe cleanup.
**Reserve external tables for interoperability:** Use them only when files are shared with other tools or must outlive the table definition.
**Apply least privilege with GRANT/REVOKE:** Grant SELECT/MODIFY narrowly and prefer schema-level grants for broad read access.
**Own tables with groups or service principals:** Avoid individual ownership so access survives personnel changes.
engineeringStandards: Treat production DROP as destructive for managed tables and protect it with change control even though UNDROP exists.
Define table DDL, properties, ownership, and grants as code for reproducibility.
Clean up external-table files explicitly when decommissioning to prevent orphaned storage.
designRecommendations: Use views to expose curated subsets and column masks/row filters for sensitive data rather than over-granting on base tables.
Choose clustering/partition keys based on real query predicates, not guesses.
Enable optional table properties (CDF, deletion vectors) only when a consumer needs them.
namingConventions: Use clear, lowercase, descriptive table names within domain schemas (e.g., gold.orders, gold.dim_customer).
Prefix or suffix by layer/type where helpful (e.g., dim_, fact_) and keep names consistent across environments.
documentationStandards: Add COMMENTs to tables and columns describing meaning and sensitivity.
Document whether each table is managed or external and why, including the external location for external tables.
Record ownership and the grant model (which groups have SELECT/MODIFY).
testingStrategies: Verify the full privilege chain (USE CATALOG -> USE SCHEMA -> SELECT/MODIFY) with a test principal.
Test DROP/UNDROP behavior in a non-prod environment to confirm managed-vs-external semantics.
Validate that external tables point at the intended external location and that DROP leaves files intact.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming dropping an external table frees its storage.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers expect DROP to always delete files, as it does for managed tables.
commonMistakes.impact: Orphaned files accumulate at the external location, silently increasing storage cost.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Remember external DROP removes metadata only; delete the files explicitly in cloud storage when truly decommissioning.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using external tables for everyday pipeline outputs.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Habit from legacy Hive setups where most tables were external.
commonMistakes.impact: You lose automatic optimization and safe cleanup, and take on manual storage management.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Default to managed tables for pipeline outputs; reserve external tables for genuine interoperability needs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Revoking SELECT on a table but access still works.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The principal retains SELECT inherited from the parent schema or catalog.
commonMistakes.impact: A 'revoked' user can still read the table, creating a false sense of security.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Check inherited grants with SHOW GRANTS and revoke at the appropriate level (schema/catalog) or restructure grants.

comparisonSection.explanation: A managed table stores files in a Unity-Catalog-controlled managed location and DROP deletes both metadata and files (recoverable via UNDROP within retention). An external table stores files at a user-specified external location and DROP removes only metadata, leaving files intact — which avoids accidental loss but risks orphaned storage.

comparisonSection.feature: Where GRANT applies and how it inherits
comparisonSection.explanation: A schema-level grant (e.g., GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA) covers all current and future tables in the schema, minimizing ACL sprawl for broad access. A table-level grant targets a single table for fine-grained control. A table also inherits whatever the schema and catalog grant, so revoking at the table level may not remove inherited access.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a managed and an external table in Unity Catalog?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A managed table has its files governed and lifecycle-controlled by Unity Catalog in a managed location, so DROP deletes the files. An external table's files live at a user-specified external location; DROP removes only the metadata and leaves the files in place.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Lead with storage ownership and DROP behavior — that is the crux of the distinction.

beginnerQuestions.question: What format do Unity Catalog managed tables use by default?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Delta Lake, which provides ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and optimization features.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Mention Delta is the default and enables the governance/optimization features UC relies on.

intermediateQuestions.question: What happens to the data when you DROP a managed table versus an external table?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Dropping a managed table removes its metadata and deletes its underlying files (recoverable via UNDROP within the retention window). Dropping an external table removes only the metadata; the files at the external location remain untouched.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is the single most common UC table interview question — be precise about both cases and mention UNDROP.

intermediateQuestions.question: You revoked SELECT on a table but the user can still read it. Why?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The user still holds SELECT inherited from the parent schema or catalog. Table-level REVOKE does not remove a grant made at a higher level; you must revoke at the level where it was granted.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding of privilege inheritance across the hierarchy.

intermediateQuestions.question: When would you choose an external table over a managed table?
intermediateQuestions.answer: When the data files must be shared with or owned by other tools, already exist at a specific location, or must persist after the table definition is dropped. Otherwise managed tables are preferred for optimization and safe cleanup.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Frame it as interoperability and lifecycle ownership versus the managed default.

advancedQuestions.question: How does ownership interact with GRANT/REVOKE on a table, and why avoid individual owners?
advancedQuestions.answer: The table owner has full control and can grant or revoke any privilege and transfer ownership. If an individual owns the table and leaves, access management can break; assigning ownership to a group or service principal keeps control durable and auditable.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the owner-as-superuser concept plus the operational reason for group ownership.

advancedQuestions.question: What are the cost and cleanup implications of using external tables at scale?
advancedQuestions.answer: Because DROP leaves files behind, external tables can leave orphaned data that continues to incur storage cost unless explicitly deleted. At scale this requires a deliberate cleanup process, whereas managed tables auto-clean on DROP and auto-optimize file layout.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connect DROP semantics to real cost/operations consequences.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A teammate dropped a critical production managed table by mistake an hour ago. Dashboards are failing. What do you do, and how would you prevent recurrence?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Recall that managed-table DROP is recoverable via UNDROP within the retention window. Act fast to UNDROP, verify data and grants, then re-point dashboards. For prevention, add change control, restrict DROP via least-privilege ownership, and consider table protections.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Run UNDROP TABLE on the managed table immediately to recover it (and its data) within the retention window, then verify grants/ownership and data integrity. Prevent recurrence by limiting MODIFY/ownership to a controlled group, gating DROPs behind change control, and using IaC so the table can be recreated if needed.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the table strategy for a lakehouse that has internal pipeline outputs plus several partner datasets that live in partner-owned buckets, with least-privilege access and predictable cleanup.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Make internal outputs managed Delta tables in domain/medallion schemas for automatic optimization and safe cleanup. Register partner data as external tables under controlled external locations so DROP never deletes partner files. Govern with schema-level grants for broad reads and table-level grants/masks for sensitive data; own tables with groups.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Managed gives optimization and auto-cleanup but destructive DROP; external gives interoperability and non-destructive DROP but manual cleanup and external-location setup. Schema grants reduce sprawl but can over-expose; table grants are precise but numerous.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Use predictive optimization for managed tables, define everything as code, audit via system tables, and establish a cleanup process for any external-table files to control orphaned-storage cost.

What is the difference between a view and a table in governance terms?
How do row filters and column masks complement table-level grants?
What does DESCRIBE EXTENDED tell you about a table's type and location?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A Unity Catalog table is a leaf securable (catalog.schema.table) holding Delta data; managed tables are Databricks-owned (DROP deletes files) while external tables point at user-owned locations (DROP keeps files).
keyConcepts: Managed = UC owns files; DROP deletes data (UNDROP within retention).
External = files at external location; DROP keeps files.
Default format is Delta with ACID + time travel.
GRANT/REVOKE at table level; grants also inherit from schema/catalog.
Owner has full control; prefer group/service-principal ownership.
commands: CREATE TABLE c.s.t (...) USING DELTA;  -- managed
GRANT SELECT, MODIFY ON TABLE c.s.t TO `group`;  REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE c.s.t FROM `group`;
DROP TABLE c.s.t;  UNDROP TABLE c.s.t;  -- UNDROP for managed within retention
ALTER TABLE c.s.t OWNER TO `team`;  DESCRIBE EXTENDED c.s.t;
interviewPoints: Managed vs external is about storage ownership and DROP behavior.
DROP deletes files only for managed tables.
UNDROP recovers managed tables within the retention window.
Revoking at table level doesn't remove schema/catalog-inherited grants.
Default to managed; use external for interoperability.
quickNotes: Table types: managed Delta, external, views, and streaming tables/materialized views.
External tables must reside under an authorized external location with a valid storage credential.
Use column masks and row filters for sensitive data instead of broad table grants.
Predictive optimization auto-compacts and clusters managed Delta tables.
Dropping an external table can leave orphaned files that still cost money.

keyTakeaways: Unity Catalog tables are leaf securables in catalog.schema.table; managed tables are Databricks-owned end-to-end while external tables only have their metadata governed.
The defining difference is storage ownership and DROP behavior: dropping a managed table deletes its files (UNDROP within retention), while dropping an external table leaves the files intact.
Tables default to Delta Lake, giving ACID transactions, time travel, schema enforcement, and automatic optimization for managed tables.
Access is controlled with table-level GRANT/REVOKE plus inherited schema/catalog grants, so a table-level revoke may not remove inherited access; prefer group/service-principal ownership.
Default to managed tables for pipeline outputs and reserve external tables for interoperability, remembering that external tables require explicit file cleanup to avoid orphaned storage cost.
